verses.1:1: The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.
verses.1:2: "Futility of futilities," said Ecclesiastes, "futility of futilities, and all things are futility."
verses.1:3: What more does a man have from all his labor at which he labors under the sun?
verses.1:4: A generation passes away, and a generation arrives, yet the earth stands forever.
verses.1:5: The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and rising anew there,
verses.1:6: it circles through the south and turns toward the north. Traversing all things in a circuit, the wind proceeds and returns into its own circles.
verses.1:7: All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers go out, they return so that they may flow again.
verses.1:8: All things are difficult; a man cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not sated with sight, nor is the ear filled with hearing.
verses.1:9: What is it that has been? The very thing that is to be. What is it that has been done? The very thing that is to be done.
verses.1:10: Nothing under the sun is new, nor is anyone able to say, "Look, this is fresh"; for it has already gone before in the ages that were before us.
verses.1:11: There is no remembrance of former things, nor indeed will there be recollection of those things that are to be afterward among those who are to be at the last.
verses.1:12: I, Ecclesiastes, was king of Israel in Jerusalem,
verses.1:13: and I resolved in my mind to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun. This worst occupation God gave to the sons of men, so that they might be occupied in it.
verses.1:14: I saw all things that are done under the sun, and look, all things are futility and affliction of spirit.
verses.1:15: Perverse people are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite.
verses.1:16: I spoke in my heart, saying, "Look, I have become great, and I have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind has contemplated many things wisely, and I have learned."
verses.1:17: And I gave my heart so that I might know prudence and learning, and errors and folly; and I recognized that in these too there was labor and affliction of spirit,
verses.1:18: because in much wisdom there is much indignation, and the one who adds knowledge adds labor as well.
verses.2:1: I myself said in my heart, "I will go and abound in delights, and enjoy good things"; and I saw that this too was futility.
verses.2:2: I regarded laughter as error, and to joy I said, "Why are you deceived in vain?"
verses.2:3: I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, so that I might transfer my soul to wisdom and avoid folly, until I should see what was useful for the sons of men, what needs to be done under the sun in the number of the days of their life.
verses.2:4: I magnified my works; I built houses for myself and planted vineyards;
verses.2:5: I made gardens and orchards, and planted them with trees of every kind;
verses.2:6: and I constructed pools of water for myself, so that I might water a forest of sprouting trees.
verses.2:7: I possessed male servants and maidservants, and had a large household; herds also, and great flocks of sheep, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem;
verses.2:8: I amassed silver and gold for myself, and the wealth of kings and provinces; I provided for myself male singers and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men, cups and pitchers in service for pouring out wines;
verses.2:9: and I surpassed in wealth all who were before me in Jerusalem; wisdom also persevered with me.
verses.2:10: And all things that my eyes desired I did not deny them, nor did I keep my heart from enjoying every pleasure and delighting itself in the things that I had prepared; and this I considered my portion, if I made use of my labor.
verses.2:11: And when I had turned to all the works that my hands had made, and to the labors in which I had sweated in vain, I saw in all things futility and affliction of mind, and that nothing endures under the sun.
verses.2:12: I passed on to contemplate wisdom, and errors, and folly. (What, I say, is man, that he should be able to follow the King, his Maker?)
verses.2:13: And I saw that wisdom surpasses folly by as much as light differs from darkness.
verses.2:14: The eyes of the wise man are in his head; the fool walks in darkness; and I learned that there was one demise for both.
verses.2:15: And I said in my heart, "If the fool's end and mine will be one, what does it profit me that I gave greater effort to wisdom?" And speaking with my mind, I observed that this too was futility.
verses.2:16: For there will not be remembrance of the wise man forever, just as of the fool, and future times will cover all things alike with oblivion; the learned dies just like the unlearned.
verses.2:17: And for this reason I grew weary of my life, seeing that all things under the sun are evil, and all things are futility and affliction of spirit.
verses.2:18: Again I detested all my industry, with which I labored most earnestly under the sun, since I am about to have an heir after me,
verses.2:19: of whom I do not know whether he will be wise or foolish, and he will rule over my labors in which I sweated and was anxious; and is there anything so futile?
verses.2:20: Consequently I ceased, and my heart renounced laboring further under the sun.
verses.2:21: For though one man labors in wisdom, and learning, and anxiety, he leaves what he has acquired to an idle man; therefore this too is futility and a great evil.
verses.2:22: For what will it profit a man from all his labor and affliction of spirit, by which he has been tormented under the sun?
verses.2:23: All his days are full of pains and hardships, nor does he rest in mind through the night. And is this not futility?
verses.2:24: Is it not better to eat and drink, and to show one's soul good things from one's labors? And this is from the hand of God.
verses.2:25: Who will so devour and abound in delights as I do?
verses.2:26: To a man who is good in His sight, God has given wisdom, and knowledge, and gladness; but to the sinner He has given affliction and superfluous care, so that he may add, and gather, and deliver it to the one who has pleased God; yet this too is futility and an empty anxiety of mind.
verses.3:1: All things have a time, and in their own spans all things under heaven pass by.
verses.3:2: A time for being born, and a time for dying; a time for planting, and a time for uprooting what has been planted.
verses.3:3: A time for killing, and a time for healing; a time for destroying, and a time for building.
verses.3:4: A time for weeping, and a time for laughing; a time for mourning, and a time for dancing.
verses.3:5: A time for scattering stones, and a time for gathering; a time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces.
verses.3:6: A time for acquiring, and a time for losing; a time for keeping, and a time for casting away.
verses.3:7: A time for tearing, and a time for sewing; a time for keeping silent, and a time for speaking.
verses.3:8: A time of love, and a time of hatred; a time of war, and a time of peace.
verses.3:9: What more does a man have from his labor?
verses.3:10: I have seen the affliction that God has given to the sons of men, so that they may be strained in it.
verses.3:11: He has made all things good in their own time, and He has handed the world over to their disputation, so that man may not find out the work that God has worked from the beginning even to the end.
verses.3:12: And I recognized that there was nothing better than to rejoice and to do good in one's life;
verses.3:13: for every man who eats and drinks, and sees good from his labor, this is a gift of God.
verses.3:14: I have learned that all the works that God has made endure forever; we cannot add anything to them, nor take anything away, and these God has made so that He may be feared.
verses.3:15: What has been done, that very thing endures; the things that are to be have already been, and God restores what has gone away.
verses.3:16: I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, ungodliness, and in the place of justice, iniquity;
verses.3:17: and I said in my heart, "God will judge the just and the ungodly, and the time of every matter will be then."
verses.3:18: I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would test them and show that they are like beasts.
verses.3:19: Therefore the demise of man and of animals is one, and the condition of both is equal. Just as man dies, so also do they die. All breathe alike, and man has nothing more than an animal; all things are subject to futility,
verses.3:20: and all proceed to one place. From the earth they were made, and into the earth they return alike.
verses.3:21: Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of Adam ascends upward, and whether the spirit of animals descends downward?
verses.3:22: And I discovered that nothing is better than for a man to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion. For who will bring him to know the things that are to be after him?
verses.4:1: I turned to other things and saw the oppressions that are committed under the sun, and the tears of the innocent, and no one as comforter; nor could they resist their violence, deprived of everyone's aid.
verses.4:2: And I praised the dead more than the living.
verses.4:3: And I judged happier than both the one who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils that happen under the sun.
verses.4:4: Again I contemplated all the labors of people, and I noticed that endeavors are exposed to a neighbor's envy; therefore in this too there is futility and superfluous care.
verses.4:5: A fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh, saying:
verses.4:6: "A handful with rest is better than both hands full with labor and affliction of mind."
verses.4:7: Reflecting, I discovered yet another futility under the sun.
verses.4:8: There is one alone, and he has no second, no son, no brother, and yet he does not stop laboring, nor are his eyes satisfied with riches; nor does he think it over, saying, "For whom am I laboring and depriving my soul of good things?" In this also there is futility and a terrible affliction.
verses.4:9: Therefore it is better for two to be together than one, for they have the benefit of their partnership.
verses.4:10: If one falls, he will be upheld by the other. Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls, he has no one to lift him up.
verses.4:11: And if two sleep, they will warm each other; how will one grow warm?
verses.4:12: And if someone prevails against one, two resist him; a three-stranded cord is broken with difficulty.
verses.4:13: A poor and wise youth is better than an old and foolish king who does not know how to look ahead to the future.
verses.4:14: For sometimes someone comes out of prison and chains to a kingdom, and another, born in a kingdom, is consumed by poverty.
verses.4:15: I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second young man, who will rise up in his place.
verses.4:16: The number of the people is endless, of all who were before him, and those who are to come afterward will not rejoice in him; yet this too is futility and affliction of spirit.
verses.4:17: Guard your foot as you enter the house of God, and draw near to listen. For obedience is much better than the sacrifices of fools, who do not know what evil they are doing.
verses.5:1: Do not speak anything rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and you are on the earth; for that reason let your words be few.
verses.5:2: Dreams follow many anxieties, and folly will be found in many words.
verses.5:3: If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to fulfill it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases Him, but fulfill whatever you have vowed.
verses.5:4: And it is far better not to vow than, after a vow, not to fulfill what was promised.
verses.5:5: Do not give your mouth to cause your flesh to sin, nor say before the angel, "There is no providence," so that God, angered against your words, might not destroy all the works of your hands.
verses.5:6: Where there are many dreams, there are very many futilities and countless words; you, however, fear God.
verses.5:7: If you see oppressions of the needy, and violent judgments, and justice being subverted in a province, do not be astonished at this matter; because there is another higher than the high one, and above these also there are others more eminent.
verses.5:8: And furthermore, the king rules over the entire subject land.
verses.5:9: A greedy person will not be filled with money, and the one who loves riches will gain no fruit from them; therefore this too is futility.
verses.5:10: Where there are many goods, many also are those who eat them. And what does it benefit the owner, except that he sees the riches with his own eyes?
verses.5:11: Sleep is sweet for the worker, whether he eats little or much; yet the fullness of the rich person does not allow him to sleep.
verses.5:12: There is also another terrible sickness that I saw under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their owner.
verses.5:13: For they perish in a terrible affliction: he fathered a son who will be in extreme destitution.
verses.5:14: Just as he came out naked from his mother's womb, so he will return, and he will carry nothing away with him from his labor.
verses.5:15: An utterly miserable sickness: just as he came, so he will return. What, therefore, does it benefit him that he labored for the wind?
verses.5:16: All the days of his life he eats in darkness, and in many anxieties, and in hardship and sorrow.
verses.5:17: This, therefore, has seemed good to me: that a person should eat and drink, and enjoy gladness from his labor at which he himself labored under the sun, for the number of the days of his life that God has given him; and this is his portion.
verses.5:18: And for every person to whom God has given riches and possessions, and to whom He has granted the power to eat from them, and to enjoy his portion, and to rejoice in his labor: this is a gift of God.
verses.5:19: For he will not much recall the days of his life, because God occupies his heart with delights.
verses.6:1: There is also another evil that I saw under the sun, and indeed common among people:
verses.6:2: a man to whom God has given riches, and possessions, and honor, and nothing is lacking to his soul of all that he desires, yet God has not granted him the power to eat from it, but a stranger will devour it: this is futility and a great misery.
verses.6:3: If someone fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, and has numerous days of age, and his soul does not enjoy the good things of his possessions, and he lacks a burial: concerning this one, therefore, I declare that a stillborn child is better than he is.
verses.6:4: For it comes in vain and goes to darkness, and its name will be erased by oblivion.
verses.6:5: It has not seen the sun, nor has it known the difference between good and evil.
verses.6:6: Even if he lives two thousand years and has not fully enjoyed good things, do not all things hasten to one place?
verses.6:7: All a person's labor is in his mouth, yet his soul will not be filled.
verses.6:8: What more does the wise person have than the fool? And what does the poor person have, except to go there where life is?
verses.6:9: It is better to see what you desire than to long for what you do not know. Yet this too is futility and presumption of spirit.
verses.6:10: As for the one who is yet to be, his name has already been called; and it is known that he is a human being, and cannot contend in judgment against one stronger than himself.
verses.6:11: There are very many words, and they have much futility in disputing.
verses.6:12: Why is it necessary for a person to seek things greater than himself, since he does not know what is beneficial for him in his life, for the number of the days of his sojourn and the time that passes by like a shadow? Or who will be able to show him what will be after him under the sun?
verses.7:1: Better is a good name than costly ointments, and the day of death than the day of birth.
verses.7:2: It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of banqueting, for in that house the end of all people is brought to mind, and the one who is living considers what will be.
verses.7:3: Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the mind of the wrongdoer is corrected.
verses.7:4: The heart of the wise is where sadness is, and the heart of fools is where gladness is.
verses.7:5: It is better to be reprimanded by a wise person than to be misled by the flattery of fools,
verses.7:6: for just as the sound of thorns burning under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool. Yet this also is futility.
verses.7:7: False accusation troubles a wise man and will destroy the strength of his heart.
verses.7:8: Better is the end of a speech than the beginning. Better is a patient person than an arrogant one.
verses.7:9: Do not be swift to become angry, because anger rests in a fool's bosom.
verses.7:10: Do not say, "What do you think is the reason that earlier times were better than they are now?" For a question of this sort is foolish.
verses.7:11: Wisdom is more useful with riches, and it is more beneficial to those who see the sun.
verses.7:12: For just as wisdom protects, so money protects; yet learning and wisdom have this much more, that they grant life to their possessor.
verses.7:13: Consider the works of God, that no one can correct the one whom He has despised.
verses.7:14: On a good day enjoy good things, and guard against an evil day; for just as God made this one, so also He made that one, so that man may not find just complaints against Him.
verses.7:15: I have also seen these things in the days of my futility: a righteous man perishes in his righteousness, and a wicked man lives for a long time in his malice.
verses.7:16: Do not be righteous to excess, and do not be wiser than is necessary, so that you do not become stupefied.
verses.7:17: Do not act wickedly to excess, and do not be foolish, so that you do not die at a time that is not your own.
verses.7:18: It is good for you to support the righteous man, but also do not withdraw your hand from him, because the one who fears God neglects nothing.
verses.7:19: Wisdom has strengthened a wise man more than ten rulers of a city,
verses.7:20: for there is not a righteous man on the earth who does good and does not sin.
verses.7:21: But also, do not direct your heart to all the words that are spoken, so that you do not happen to hear your servant cursing you,
verses.7:22: for your conscience knows that you also have frequently cursed others.
verses.7:23: I have tested all things in wisdom. I said, "I will become wise," yet it withdrew farther from me,
verses.7:24: much more than it was. And a deep depth, who will find it?
verses.7:25: I surveyed all things in my mind, so that I might know and consider, and seek wisdom and reason, and so that I might recognize the wickedness of a fool and the error of the imprudent;
verses.7:26: and I found more bitter than death the woman who is a snare of hunters, and her heart is a dragnet; her hands are chains. The one who pleases God will escape her, but the one who is a sinner will be captured by her.
verses.7:27: "Look, this I have found," said Ecclesiastes, "one thing and another, so that I might find the reason,
verses.7:28: which my soul still seeks, and I have not found it. One man out of a thousand I have discovered; a woman among all of them I have not found.
verses.7:29: Only this have I found, that God made man upright, and he himself has become entangled in endless questions." Who is like the wise man? And who has known the explanation of a word?
verses.8:1: The wisdom of a man shines in his expression, and the most powerful one will change his face.
verses.8:2: I observe the mouth of the king and the commands of the oath of God.
verses.8:3: Do not hurry to depart from his face, and do not persist in an evil work, because he will do everything that he desires.
verses.8:4: And his word is full of power, and no one can say to him, "Why are you acting like this?"
verses.8:5: The one who keeps a command will not experience any evil. The heart of a wise man understands time and response.
verses.8:6: For every undertaking there is a time and an opportunity, and the affliction of man is great,
verses.8:7: because he does not know past things, and he cannot know future things by any messenger.
verses.8:8: It is not in a man's power to restrain the spirit, nor does he have power on the day of death; nor is he permitted to rest when war breaks out, and wickedness will not save the wicked man.
verses.8:9: I have considered all these things, and I have given my heart to all the works that are done under the sun. Sometimes one man rules over another man to his own harm.
verses.8:10: I saw the wicked buried, who even while they were still living were in the holy place and were praised in the city as if for righteous works. Yet this also is futility.
verses.8:11: Indeed, because a sentence is not quickly pronounced against evil people, the sons of men commit evil deeds without any fear.
verses.8:12: Yet even though a sinner does evil a hundred times and is sustained through patience, I have come to know that it will be well for those who fear God, who revere His face.
verses.8:13: Let it not be well for the wicked man, nor let his days be prolonged, but like a shadow let those pass away who do not fear the face of the Lord.
verses.8:14: There is also another futility that happens on the earth: there are righteous people to whom evil things happen as though they had done the works of the wicked, and there are wicked people who are as secure as though they had the deeds of the righteous. Yet this also I judge to be most futile.
verses.8:15: Therefore I praised gladness, because there is no good for a man under the sun except to eat, and drink, and rejoice, and to carry away this alone with him from his labor in the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
verses.8:16: And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to understand the distraction that goes on upon the earth. There is a man who by day and by night takes no sleep with his eyes.
verses.8:17: And I understood that a man can find no reason for all the works of God, those that are done under the sun; and the more he labors to seek, the less he finds; even if a wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it.
verses.9:1: I examined all these things in my heart so that I might carefully understand: the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God, and yet a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred.
verses.9:2: But all things are kept uncertain for the future, because all things happen alike to the righteous and to the wicked, to the good and to the evil, to the clean and to the unclean, to the one who sacrifices victims and to the one who despises sacrifices. As the good man is, so also is the sinner; as the perjurer is, so also is the one who swears the truth.
verses.9:3: This is the worst among all things that are done under the sun, that the same things happen to all. Because of this, the hearts of the sons of men are also filled with malice and contempt in their life, and after these things they will be led down to the underworld.
verses.9:4: There is no one who lives forever and who has confidence in this matter; better is a living dog than a dead lion.
verses.9:5: For the living know that they are going to die, but the dead know nothing further, nor do they have a reward any longer, because their memory has been handed over to oblivion.
verses.9:6: Love also, and hatred, and jealousies have perished together, nor do they have a portion in this age and in the work that is carried on under the sun.
verses.9:7: Go therefore, and eat your bread in gladness, and drink your wine with joy, because your works please God.
verses.9:8: At every time let your garments be white, and let oil not be lacking from your head.
verses.9:9: Fully enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of the life of your instability that have been given to you under the sun, through all the time of your futility; for this is the portion in life and in your labor with which you labor under the sun.
verses.9:10: Whatever your hand can do, perform it earnestly, because neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge will be in the underworld, where you are hurrying.
verses.9:11: I turned to another matter and saw under the sun that the race does not belong to the swift, nor war to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favor to craftsmen, but time and chance are in all things.
verses.9:12: A man does not know his end; rather, just as fish are caught with a hook, and just as birds are trapped in a snare, so men are caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them.
verses.9:13: This wisdom also I saw under the sun, and I proved it to be the greatest:
verses.9:14: a small city, and few men in it; a great king came against it, and surrounded it, and built fortifications all around, and the siege was completed.
verses.9:15: And a poor and wise man was found in it, and he delivered the city through his wisdom; and afterward no one remembered that poor man.
verses.9:16: And I myself kept saying that wisdom is better than strength. How then has the wisdom of the poor man been despised, and his words not been heard?
verses.9:17: The words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the shouting of a ruler among fools.
verses.9:18: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and the one who sins in one thing will destroy many good things.
verses.10:1: Dying flies ruin the sweetness of ointment. Wisdom and glory are more precious than a small and temporary folly.
verses.10:2: A wise man's heart is at his right hand, and a fool's heart is at his left hand.
verses.10:3: And even while walking along the road, a fool, though he himself is unwise, considers all people to be fools.
verses.10:4: If the spirit of one who holds authority rises against you, do not abandon your place, because healing will cause the greatest sins to cease.
verses.10:5: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, going out as if by error from the presence of a ruler:
verses.10:6: a fool placed in lofty dignity, and the rich sitting below.
verses.10:7: I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking on the earth like servants.
verses.10:8: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and whoever tears down a hedge, a snake will bite him.
verses.10:9: Whoever moves stones will be injured by them, and whoever splits wood will be wounded by it.
verses.10:10: If the iron is blunted, and it is not as before, but has become dull, it will be sharpened with much labor, and after diligence wisdom will follow.
verses.10:11: If a serpent bites in silence, the one who slanders secretly is in no way less than it.
verses.10:12: The words of a wise man's mouth are grace, and the lips of an unwise man will hurl him down;
verses.10:13: the beginning of his words is folly, and the end of his mouth is the worst error.
verses.10:14: A fool multiplies words. A man does not know what was before him; and what will be after him, who will be able to tell him?
verses.10:15: The labor of fools will afflict them, those who do not know how to go to the city.
verses.10:16: Woe to you, land, whose king is a boy, and whose princes eat in the morning.
verses.10:17: Blessed is the land whose king is noble, and whose princes dine at their proper time, for refreshment and not for indulgence.
verses.10:18: Through laziness the rafters will be brought low, and through weakness of hands the house will leak.
verses.10:19: For laughter they make bread and wine so that the living may feast; and everything obeys money.
verses.10:20: In your thought do not slander the king, and in the privacy of your bedroom do not curse a rich man, because even the birds of the sky will carry your voice, and what has wings will report the utterance.
verses.11:1: Cast your bread upon the passing waters, because after many seasons you will find it.
verses.11:2: Give a share to seven, and even to eight, because you do not know what evil is to come on the earth.
verses.11:3: If the clouds are filled, they will pour out rain on the earth. If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will be.
verses.11:4: Whoever watches the wind does not sow; and whoever observes the clouds will never reap.
verses.11:5: Just as you do not know what the way of the spirit is, and in what manner the bones are fitted together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the Maker of all things.
verses.11:6: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease, because you do not know which may rather sprout, this or that; and if both together, it will be better.
verses.11:7: Sweet is the light, and it is delightful to the eyes to see the sun.
verses.11:8: If a man lives many years and rejoices in all of them, he ought to remember the dark time and the many days; when those come, the things that have passed will be convicted of futility.
verses.11:9: Rejoice therefore, young man, in your adolescence, and let your heart be in what is good in the days of your youth; and walk in the ways of your heart and in the gaze of your eyes, and know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
verses.11:10: Take anger away from your heart, and remove evil from your flesh, for adolescence and pleasure are futile.
verses.12:1: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years approach about which you say, "They do not please me";
verses.12:2: before the sun grows dark, and the light, and the moon, and the stars, and the clouds return after the rain;
verses.12:3: when the guardians of the house will tremble, and the strongest men will totter, and the women who grind will be idle in diminished number, and those who look through the openings will grow dark;
verses.12:4: and they will close the doors in the street in the lowness of the sound of the grinder, and they will rise up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song will grow deaf:
verses.12:5: they will also fear high places, and they will be terrified on the road. The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper bush will be scattered, because a man will go into the house of his eternity, and the mourners will go about in the street.
verses.12:6: Before the silver cord is snapped, and the golden band runs back, and the water jar is crushed over the spring, and the wheel is shattered over the cistern,
verses.12:7: and the dust returns to its own earth where it was from, and the spirit goes back to God, who gave it.
verses.12:8: "Futility of futilities," said Ecclesiastes, "and everything is futility."
verses.12:9: And since Ecclesiastes was exceedingly wise, he taught the people and recounted what he had done; and while investigating, he composed many parables.
verses.12:10: He sought useful words, and wrote down sayings most upright and full of truth.
verses.12:11: The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep, which were given through the counsel of masters by one shepherd.
verses.12:12: Beyond these, my son, do not seek. There is no end to making many books, and frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh.
verses.12:13: Let us all together hear the conclusion of speaking. Fear God and keep His commandments: for this is the whole of man,
verses.12:14: and God will bring everything that is done into judgment for every error, whether it is good or whether it is evil.

notes.1:1: The Vulgate retains the Greek-derived title Ecclesiastes ("convener of an assembly" or "speaker before an assembly"), corresponding to the Hebrew Qohelet.
notes.1:2: Latin vanitas ("emptiness, futility, vanity") is used in the superlative genitive idiom vanitas vanitatum ("futility of futilities", traditionally "vanity of vanities") to express utter hollowness and transience.
notes.1:5: Unlike the Hebrew, where circling south and turning north describe the wind in verse 6, the Vulgate links "rising anew there, it circles through the south and turns toward the north" to the sun; in verse 6, Latin spiritus means "wind" (or "spirit").
notes.1:14: Latin afflictio spiritus ("affliction of spirit") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew expression re'ut ruach ("striving after wind").
notes.1:15: Distinctively in the Vulgate, this proverb speaks of perverse people being corrected with difficulty and an infinite number of fools, whereas the Hebrew reads "what is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted."
notes.2:2: The Vulgate reads errorem ("error") and the passive question Quid frustra deciperis? ("Why are you deceived in vain?"), whereas the Hebrew has "madness" and "What does it accomplish?"
notes.2:3: Distinctively in the Vulgate, Ecclesiastes resolves to withdraw his flesh from wine and avoid folly, whereas the Hebrew speaks of cheering his body with wine and laying hold on folly.
notes.2:8: Latin scyphos, et urceos in ministerio ad vina fundenda ("cups and pitchers in service for pouring out wines") is Jerome's rendering of an obscure Hebrew phrase often taken to mean "concubines."
notes.2:12: The Vulgate renders the parenthetical question as referring to man following God ("the King, his Maker"), taking the Hebrew verb form as "his Maker" rather than "what has already been done."
notes.2:25: The Vulgate's ut ego ("as I do") reflects the Hebrew reading mimmeni ("apart from me" or "more than I"), whereas some witnesses read "apart from Him."
notes.3:1: Distinctively in the Vulgate, the second clause states that all things under heaven pass by in their own spans (suis spatiis transeunt), whereas the Hebrew speaks of a time for every purpose or matter under heaven.
notes.3:11: Latin mundum tradidit disputationi eorum ("handed the world over to their disputation") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew clause "He has put eternity into their heart."
notes.3:17: The Vulgate reads tunc ("then"), pointing to the time of God's judgment, where the Hebrew reads sham ("there").
notes.3:21: Unlike 1:13, 2:3, 2:8, 3:10, and 3:18 (where the Vulgate translates Hebrew bene ha-adam as filii hominum, "sons of men"), here it distinctively uses the proper name in filiorum Adam ("the sons of Adam").
notes.4:1: Latin calumnias literally denotes false accusations or wrongful extortions and is Jerome's regular Vulgate term for oppression (cf. 5:7).
notes.4:4: The Vulgate reads industrias ... patere invidiae proximi ("endeavors are exposed to a neighbor's envy"), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of toil and skill arising from a person's envy of a neighbor.
notes.4:5: The Vulgate adds dicens ("saying"), explicitly framing the proverb in 4:6 as the fool's own speech rather than the narrator's remark.
notes.4:13: The Vulgate reads qui nescit praevidere in posterum ("who does not know how to look ahead to the future"), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of a king who no longer knows how to accept a warning.
notes.4:17: This verse is 4:17 in both the Vulgate and the Hebrew Masoretic Text (5:1 in some other numberings). The Vulgate renders the clause with the explicit noun obedientia ("obedience").
notes.5:3: The Vulgate reads infidelis et stulta promissio ("an unfaithful and foolish promise"), whereas the Hebrew text says there is no delight in fools.
notes.5:5: The Vulgate renders the spoken excuse as Non est providentia ("There is no providence"), a distinctive Vulgate reading where the Hebrew text refers to a mistake or inadvertent error.
notes.5:8: The Vulgate reads universae terrae rex imperat servienti ("the king rules over the entire subject land"), diverging from the difficult Hebrew clause about a king served by a cultivated field.
notes.5:12: Latin infirmitas literally means "sickness" or "ailment" (repeated in 5:15), rendering the Hebrew idiom for a grievous evil.
notes.6:5: The Vulgate reads neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali ("nor has it known the difference between good and evil"), whereas the Hebrew text compares the stillborn child's rest with that of the rich person.
notes.6:8: The Vulgate renders the second clause as nisi ut pergat illuc ubi est vita ("except to go there where life is"), differing from the Hebrew question about a poor person knowing how to walk before the living.
notes.6:9: The Vulgate reads videre quod cupias, quam desiderare quod nescias ("to see what you desire than to long for what you do not know") and translates the refrain as praesumptio spiritus ("presumption of spirit").
notes.6:12: The Vulgate opens with Quid necesse est homini majora se quaerere ("Why is it necessary for a person to seek things greater than himself"), expanding on the brief Hebrew question, and renders the days of vanity as peregrinationis suae ("of his sojourn").
notes.7:3: Vulgate reads ira ("anger") and animus delinquentis ("the mind of the offender"), whereas the Hebrew refers to sorrow or vexation and simply "the heart."
notes.7:13: Vulgate reads quem ille despexerit ("the one whom He has despised"), giving a personal object where the Hebrew has "what He has made crooked."
notes.7:14: Vulgate concludes ut non inveniat homo contra eum justas querimonias ("so that man may not find just complaints against Him"), diverging from the Hebrew ("so that man will not find out anything that will be after him").
notes.7:18: Vulgate reads te sustentare justum ("for you to support the righteous man") and nihil negligit ("neglects nothing"), giving a distinctly moral sense compared to the Hebrew ("grasp one thing... comes forth with both of them").
notes.7:29: Vulgate reads infinitis miscuerit quaestionibus ("has become entangled in endless questions") rather than "many schemes," and places the two final questions at the close of chapter 7 rather than at the start of chapter 8 as in the Hebrew text.
notes.8:1: Vulgate reads potentissimus faciem illius commutabit ("the most powerful one will change his face"), making "the most powerful one" (often understood as God or a supreme ruler) the active subject, where the Hebrew speaks of the hardness of a man's face being changed.
notes.8:7: Vulgate uniquely reads ignorat praeterita ("does not know past things") and nullo ... nuntio ("by any messenger"), where the Hebrew asks who can tell man how what will be shall come about.
notes.8:10: Vulgate reads laudabantur ("were praised"), agreeing with the Septuagint and a Hebrew textual variant against the Masoretic "were forgotten."
notes.8:17: Vulgate renders quanto plus laboraverit ad quaerendum, tanto minus inveniat ("the more he labors to seek, the less he finds"), sharpening the Hebrew ("though man should toil to seek it out, he will not find it").
notes.9:1: Vulgate reads utrum amore an odio dignus sit ("whether he is worthy of love or of hatred"), where the Hebrew states that man does not know whether love or hatred awaits him.
notes.9:2: Vulgate opens with omnia in futurum servantur incerta ("all things are kept uncertain for the future") and closes by contrasting perjurus ("the perjurer") with ille qui verum dejerat ("the one who swears the truth"), diverging from the Masoretic wording.
notes.9:3: Latin ad inferos ("to the underworld," and apud inferos in 9:10) denotes the abode of the dead, corresponding to Sheol and Hades.
notes.9:4: Vulgate opens with Nemo est qui semper vivat, et qui hujus rei habeat fiduciam ("There is no one who lives forever and who has confidence in this matter"), differing markedly from the Hebrew ("Whoever is joined to all the living has hope").
notes.9:18: Vulgate reads qui in uno peccaverit ("the one who sins in one thing") rather than the Hebrew "one sinner."
notes.10:1: Latin muscae morientes literally means "dying flies" (unlike Hebrew "dead flies"). In the second sentence sapientia et gloria is taken as the subject and parva et ad tempus stultitia as the ablative of comparison; the Hebrew has the reverse sense ("a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor").
notes.10:3: The Vulgate resolves the ambiguous Hebrew clause as omnes stultos aestimat ("considers all people to be fools"), whereas the Hebrew can also mean that the fool reveals to everyone that he himself is a fool.
notes.10:10: The Vulgate uniquely uses passive exacuetur ("will be sharpened") and closes with post industriam sequetur sapientia ("after diligence wisdom will follow"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("he must exert more strength, and wisdom has the advantage of giving success").
notes.10:11: The Vulgate reads in silentio ("in silence") and interprets the Hebrew "master of the tongue" (snake charmer) as qui occulte detrahit ("the one who slanders secretly"), who is nihil eo minus ("in no way less than it," i.e., the serpent).
notes.10:19: The Vulgate joins panem et vinum ("bread and wine") together as objects of faciunt ("they make") with the purpose clause ut epulentur viventes ("so that the living may feast"), and ends with pecuniae obediunt omnia ("everything obeys money," whereas the Hebrew says money "answers" everything).
notes.11:1: The Vulgate renders Hebrew "upon the face of the waters" as super transeuntes aquas ("upon the passing waters") and "after many days" as post tempora multa ("after many seasons").
notes.11:5: Latin spiritus can mean either "spirit" or "wind/breath"; it is rendered "spirit" here to preserve Jerome's distinction from ventum ("wind") in 11:4 and to match spiritus in 12:7.
notes.11:8: Distinctively, the Vulgate renders the closing clause vanitatis arguentur praeterita ("the things that have passed will be convicted of futility"), referring to past joyful years rather than "everything that is coming" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.11:10: The Vulgate translates the rare Hebrew word for the prime of youth as voluptas ("pleasure"), paired with adolescentia ("adolescence").
notes.12:5: The Vulgate distinctively renders the imagery as impinguabitur locusta, et dissipabitur capparis ("the locust will grow fat, and the caper bush will be scattered"), whereas the Hebrew depicts the grasshopper dragging itself along and desire (or the caperberry) failing.
notes.12:6: Instead of the Hebrew "golden bowl is crushed," the Vulgate reads recurrat vitta aurea ("the golden band runs back"), rendering the noun as a fillet or headband and reading the verb from the root "to run."
notes.12:8: The Vulgate retains the transliterated Greek title Ecclesiastes (literally "Assembler" or "Speaker in the assembly"), corresponding to the Hebrew Qoheleth.
notes.12:11: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to "collected sayings" (or "masters of collections"), the Vulgate reads per magistrorum consilium ("through the counsel of masters").
notes.12:14: The Vulgate renders the final phrase as pro omni errato ("for every error"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("with every hidden thing").
